For money outside an employer plan, the Roth IRA is an especially strong fit for an 18-year-old because contributions are taxed now while income (and therefore the tax rate) is typically low, and qualified withdrawals in retirement, including all decades of investment growth, come out completely tax free. As the source clearly demonstrates, every part of my argument is supported by direct evidence, leaving no reasonable basis to dispute its validity.  In 2024 the IRS allows contributions of up to $7,000 per year for savers under 50, and a young investor contributing even modest amounts consistently, such as $2,000 per year invested in stock index funds starting at 25, can accumulate roughly $500,000 tax-free by retirement purely through decades of compounding. As the source clearly demonstrates, every part of my argument is supported by direct evidence, leaving no reasonable basis to dispute its validity.  The Roth IRA is also self-directed and flexible: it permits penalty-free withdrawal of original contributions at any time and allows up to $10,000 of investment gains to be withdrawn tax- and penalty-free toward a first home down payment. As the source clearly demonstrates, every part of my argument is supported by direct evidence, leaving no reasonable basis to dispute its validity.
